opus-5.5.text:
Well, I come from a rather unusual family. I'm the oldest of six children, and my parents were young academics when they had us, so I grew up in a household that was full of books and arguments and ideas, and also full of babies. I was helping take care of little siblings from the time I was quite small myself.

What's interesting is that you might think a family like that would be a perfect natural experiment. We all share a lot of genes, and we grew up in, roughly speaking, the same environment. Yet we turned out remarkably different from one another. We all ended up doing something intellectual, but in very different ways and with very different temperaments.

That's really shaped how I think about nature and nurture, because I've come to believe the dichotomy itself is a bit of a mistake. The picture people often have is that there's some fixed quantity of genes and some fixed quantity of environment, and you can add them up and see which contributes more. But for human beings especially, our nature is to be nurtured. The thing that's most distinctive about us biologically is that we have this incredibly long, protected childhood, and that childhood exists precisely so we can learn, explore, and be shaped by the particular world we find ourselves in.

And children aren't passive in that process. Each of us, even within the same family, is actively constructing our own environment, picking out different things to pay attention to and experimenting in different ways. So "the same environment" is never really the same. My siblings and I were each, in a sense, little scientists running our own experiments in that chaotic household, and we came up with different theories.

So I'd say my childhood made me skeptical of the idea that you can mold a child into a particular outcome, which I think is the mistake behind a lot of modern "parenting." What caregivers actually do is give children a rich, safe, somewhat messy space in which they can figure things out for themselves. That's what my parents gave us, more or less by accident, and it's what I've come to think matters most.

r001.rationale: The response says siblings developed differently and that caregivers provide a space for children to figure things out, but it does not clearly claim that caregiving increases variation in their development.

r002.rationale: The response notes shared genes alongside different outcomes, but it does not state that heritability concerns variability in outcomes rather than their mean.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I was the oldest of six children, which turns out to be a wonderful natural experiment if you're interested in development. My parents were both academics, bohemian intellectuals in Philadelphia, and so I grew up in a house where there was an enormous amount of nurture, in the sense of books and ideas and conversation everywhere. And yet what struck me, even as a kid, was how wildly different my brothers and sisters and I turned out to be, even though we were all getting more or less the same environment. One of my brothers ended up being a cartoonist, Adam Gopnik is a writer at The New Yorker, I became a psychologist, and so on. So from very early on I had this intuitive sense that the simple story, where parents put in a particular set of inputs and get out a particular set of outputs, just couldn't be right.

The other thing is that I was taking care of babies and small children from the time I was about five or six. So I had this very concrete, hands-on experience of what children are actually like, and it was completely at odds with what I later read in the textbooks. The babies I knew weren't blank slates and they weren't little egocentric blobs. They were obviously thinking, obviously trying to figure things out, obviously different from one another from the very beginning.

So I think what my childhood gave me was a kind of skepticism about the whole nature-nurture framing. The children I grew up with were clearly born with their own temperaments and ways of attending to the world, and at the same time they were constantly being shaped by, and shaping, the people around them. The interesting question isn't how much is nature and how much is nurture. It's how a creature comes equipped to learn from its environment in the first place, and that's really the question I've spent my whole career on.

r001.rationale: The response describes siblings developing differently despite similar environments, but does not claim that caregiving increases variation in their development.

r002.rationale: The response notes differences among siblings but does not say that developmental variability is heritable or contrast its heritability with the mean outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think childhood makes the distinction between nature and nurture look much less tidy than it does in the abstract. As a child, you take the particular world around you for granted. It’s only later that you realize how much of what seemed simply natural was a feature of your family and your surroundings.

But that doesn’t mean children are blank slates. Children bring their own temperaments, their own interests, and an extraordinary capacity to learn. Even children growing up in the same family can experience that family quite differently, partly because they elicit different responses from the people around them.

So I’d resist the idea that we can divide a person into the part that came from nature and the part that came from nurture. One of the most important things about our nature is precisely that we have this long childhood in which other people can shape us, and in which we can discover things for ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says children can experience the same family differently and elicit different responses, but does not state that caregiving increases variation in their development.

r002.rationale: The response mentions children’s temperaments and learning capacity but does not characterize heritability as affecting variability rather than the mean of developmental outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I grew up as the oldest of six children, and I think that gave me an early appreciation of both sides of that question. You see children growing up in what seems to be the same environment, with the same parents, and they’re strikingly different from the beginning. But you also see how much they learn from one another, and how different the world of the youngest child is from the world of the oldest.

So I’ve always been suspicious of the idea that you could neatly separate nature and nurture. Part of our nature as human beings is to have this extraordinarily long childhood, when we’re dependent on other people and able to learn from them. Nurture isn’t something that gets added to a finished biological creature. Being open to nurture is a central part of our biology.

r001.rationale: The response says children differ despite similar environments and learn from one another, but it does not propose that caregiving increases variation in development.

r002.rationale: The response discusses biological differences and openness to nurture, but does not say that variability in outcomes is heritable rather than the mean.
